claim: The cryoEM structure of rat Kv1.2 in open state was obtained at 3.2 Å resolution.
source: Focusing on the transmembrane region of the Kv1.2 channel complexes, we obtained structures of nominally open, C-type inactivated, DTx-bound, and K+-free states at resolutions of 3.2 Å, 2.5 Å, 3.2 Å, and 2.9 Å, respectively.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the resolution achieved for the open state structure.

claim: The cryoEM structure of rat Kv1.2 in C-type inactivated state was obtained at 2.5 Å resolution.
source: Focusing on the transmembrane region of the Kv1.2 channel complexes, we obtained structures of nominally open, C-type inactivated, DTx-bound, and K+-free states at resolutions of 3.2 Å, 2.5 Å, 3.2 Å, and 2.9 Å, respectively.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the resolution achieved for the C-type inactivated state structure.

claim: The cryoEM structure of rat Kv1.2 in toxin-blocked state was obtained at 3.2 Å resolution.
source: Focusing on the transmembrane region of the Kv1.2 channel complexes, we obtained structures of nominally open, C-type inactivated, DTx-bound, and K+-free states at resolutions of 3.2 Å, 2.5 Å, 3.2 Å, and 2.9 Å, respectively.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the resolution achieved for the DTx-bound state structure.

claim: The cryoEM structure of rat Kv1.2 in sodium-bound state was obtained at 2.9 Å resolution.
source: Focusing on the transmembrane region of the Kv1.2 channel complexes, we obtained structures of nominally open, C-type inactivated, DTx-bound, and K+-free states at resolutions of 3.2 Å, 2.5 Å, 3.2 Å, and 2.9 Å, respectively.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the resolution achieved for the K+-free (Na+-bound) state structure.

claim: All Kv1.2 structures were obtained at nominally zero membrane potential in detergent micelles.
source: These structures, all obtained at nominally zero membrane potential in detergent micelles, reveal distinct ion-occupancy patterns in the selectivity filter.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the experimental conditions under which structures were obtained.

claim: The toxin α-Dendrotoxin attaches to the negatively-charged channel outer mouth.
source: First, the toxin α-Dendrotoxin, like Charybdotoxin, is seen to attach to the negatively-charged channel outer mouth, and a lysine residue penetrates into the selectivity filter, with the terminal amine coordinated by carbonyls, partially disrupting the outermost ion-binding site.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly describes the binding location of α-Dendrotoxin based on structural observations.

claim: A lysine residue of α-Dendrotoxin penetrates into the selectivity filter with the terminal amine coordinated by carbonyls.
source: First, the toxin α-Dendrotoxin, like Charybdotoxin, is seen to attach to the negatively-charged channel outer mouth, and a lysine residue penetrates into the selectivity filter, with the terminal amine coordinated by carbonyls, partially disrupting the outermost ion-binding site.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly describes the mechanism of toxin block based on structural observations.

claim: In the toxin-blocked Kv1.2 channel, two densities of bound ions are observed in the selectivity filter rather than three.
source: In the remainder of the filter two densities of bound ions are observed, rather than three as observed with other toxin-blocked Kv channels.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the number of ion densities observed in the DTx-bound structure.

claim: The structure of Kv1.2 in Na+ solution shows an intact selectivity filter with ion density in each binding site.
source: Second, a structure of Kv1.2 in Na+ solution does not show collapse or destabilization of the selectivity filter, but instead shows an intact selectivity filter with ion density in each binding site.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly describes the structural observations in Na+ solution.

claim: The structure of Kv1.2 in Na+ solution does not show collapse or destabilization of the selectivity filter.
source: Second, a structure of Kv1.2 in Na+ solution does not show collapse or destabilization of the selectivity filter, but instead shows an intact selectivity filter with ion density in each binding site.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states that the selectivity filter remains intact in Na+ solution.

claim: The C-type inactivated Kv1.2 W366F channel in Na+ solution shows highly variable protein conformation.
source: We also attempted to image the C-type inactivated Kv1.2 W366F channel in Na+ solution, but the protein conformation was seen to be highly variable and only a low-resolution structure could be obtained.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly describes the structural variability observed in the W366F mutant in Na+ solution.

claim: Only a low-resolution structure could be obtained for the C-type inactivated Kv1.2 W366F channel in Na+ solution.
source: We also attempted to image the C-type inactivated Kv1.2 W366F channel in Na+ solution, but the protein conformation was seen to be highly variable and only a low-resolution structure could be obtained.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the resolution limitation for this particular structure.

claim: The Kv1.2 structure is very similar to the Shaker channel structure.
source: Structures of the Kv1.2s channel (Figure 1, Figure 1—figure supplement 1) are very similar to those of the Kv1.2–2.1 chimera (Long et al., 2007) and Drosophila Shaker (Tan et al., 2022) channels.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly compares the Kv1.2 structure to Shaker.

claim: The Kv1.2 structure is very similar to the Kv1.2–2.1 chimera structure.
source: Structures of the Kv1.2s channel (Figure 1, Figure 1—figure supplement 1) are very similar to those of the Kv1.2–2.1 chimera (Long et al., 2007) and Drosophila Shaker (Tan et al., 2022) channels.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly compares the Kv1.2 structure to the Kv1.2-2.1 chimera.

claim: The RMS difference of all Arg sidechain atoms between Kv1.2 and Shaker VSD is 0.85 Å.
source: In the critical region of the voltage-sensor domain (VSD) the sidechains of the voltage-sensing Arg and the coordinating Glu and Asp residues, as well as the charge-transfer center phenylalanine (Tao et al., 2010) are essentially superimposable with Shaker (Figure 1D), with an RMS difference of all Arg sidechain atoms of 0.85 Å.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly provides the quantitative RMS difference measurement.

claim: Kv1.2 has 68% amino-acid identity with Drosophila Shaker.
source: As Kv1.2 is a member of the Shaker potassium channel family and has 68% amino-acid identity with Drosophila Shaker, it is not surprising that the fold is very similar.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the sequence identity between Kv1.2 and Shaker.

claim: An open S6 gate is visible in the detergent-solubilized Kv1.2s structure.
source: As in the other homologues an open S6 gate is visible in the detergent-solubilized Kv1.2s structure; this is expected for the open conformation at zero membrane potential.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly describes the observation of an open S6 gate.

claim: The total gating charge movement in Shaker channels is about 13 elementary charges per channel.
source: Despite the very closely matched open-state structures of the VSDs it is therefore puzzling that the total gating charge movement in Shaker channels is larger, about 13 elementary charges per channel, while it is only 10 e0 per channel in Kv1.2 (Islas, 2016).
evidence: The manuscript cites a reference (Islas, 2016) for this measurement.

claim: The total gating charge movement in Kv1.2 channels is 10 elementary charges per channel.
source: Despite the very closely matched open-state structures of the VSDs it is therefore puzzling that the total gating charge movement in Shaker channels is larger, about 13 elementary charges per channel, while it is only 10 e0 per channel in Kv1.2 (Islas, 2016).
evidence: The manuscript cites a reference (Islas, 2016) for this measurement.

claim: The Kv1.2s-W366F mutant allows currents to flow transiently on depolarization but decay to less than 3% of the peak within 80ms.
source: While the corresponding mutation W434F in Shaker essentially abolishes ion current through the channel (Yang et al., 1997) the Kv1.2s mutant allows currents to flow transiently on depolarization, but decay to less than 3% of the peak within 80ms (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly describes the functional properties of the W366F mutant with reference to experimental data.

claim: The W434F mutation in Shaker essentially abolishes ion current through the channel.
source: While the corresponding mutation W434F in Shaker essentially abolishes ion current through the channel (Yang et al., 1997) the Kv1.2s mutant allows currents to flow transiently on depolarization, but decay to less than 3% of the peak within 80ms (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The manuscript cites Yang et al., 1997 for this functional observation.

claim: Inactivation in Kv1.2s-W366F channels can be slowed by raising extracellular K+.
source: Inactivation in these channels can be slowed by raising extracellular K+ or by applying tetraethylammonium ion (Suárez-Delgado et al., 2020), properties that are hallmarks of C-type inactivation.
evidence: The manuscript cites Suárez-Delgado et al., 2020 for this functional property.

claim: Inactivation in Kv1.2s-W366F channels can be slowed by applying tetraethylammonium ion.
source: Inactivation in these channels can be slowed by raising extracellular K+ or by applying tetraethylammonium ion (Suárez-Delgado et al., 2020), properties that are hallmarks of C-type inactivation.
evidence: The manuscript cites Suárez-Delgado et al., 2020 for this functional property.

claim: The overall conformational difference between open and inactivated structures in Kv1.2s is identical to the difference observed in structures of Shaker and Kv1.2–2.1.
source: The overall conformational difference between open and inactivated structures in Kv1.2s is identical to the difference observed in structures of Shaker (Tan et al., 2022) and in structures of Kv1.2–2.1 (Long et al., 2007; Reddi et al., 2022).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly compares the conformational changes across different channel structures with citations.

claim: The selectivity filter of potassium channels consists of an array of four copies of the extended loop formed by the sequence TTVGYGD.
source: The selectivity filter of potassium channels consists of an array of four copies of the extended loop (the P-loop) formed by a highly conserved sequence, in this case TTVGYGD.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly describes the composition of the selectivity filter.

claim: The main-chain carbonyl oxygens of residues TVGY delineate ion binding sites S3, S2 and S1.
source: The main-chain carbonyl oxygens of the residues TVGY, positions 25' to 28', delineate ion binding sites S3, S2 and S1, respectively, while the lower (most intracellular) edge of binding-site S4 is formed by the T25' hydroxyl.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly describes the structural basis of ion binding sites.

claim: The lower edge of binding-site S4 is formed by the T25' hydroxyl.
source: The main-chain carbonyl oxygens of the residues TVGY, positions 25' to 28', delineate ion binding sites S3, S2 and S1, respectively, while the lower (most intracellular) edge of binding-site S4 is formed by the T25' hydroxyl.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly describes the structural basis of the S4 binding site.

claim: Y28' is normally constrained by hydrogen bonds to residues in the pore helix and helix S6.
source: Normally, the tyrosine Y28' (Y377 in Kv1.2) is constrained by hydrogen bonds to residues in the pore helix and helix S6 and is key to the conformation of the selectivity filter.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly describes the hydrogen bonding interactions of Y28'.

claim: D30' normally participates in H-bonds with W17' on the pore helix.
source: The final aspartate of the P-loop, D30' (D379 in Kv1.2) is normally located near the extracellular surface and has a side chain that also participates in H-bonds with W17' (W366 in Kv1.2) on the pore helix.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly describes the hydrogen bonding interactions of D30'.

claim: When W17' is mutated to phenylalanine, it is no longer an H-bond donor to D30'.
source: When W17' is mutated to phenylalanine, it is no longer an H-bond donor to D30' (Figure 2D right upper panel).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly describes the effect of the W17'F mutation on hydrogen bonding.

claim: The reorientation of the phenol group of Y28' is through a pitch angle of about 120°.
source: The reorientation of the phenol group of Y28' is through a very large pitch angle of about 120° (Figure 2G,H,I).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly quantifies the conformational change of Y28'.

claim: The enlargement of ion-binding site IS2 results in a width of 5.1 Å between opposing carbonyl oxygens.
source: The result is an enlargement of the ion-binding site IS2 to a width of 5.1 Å between opposing carbonyl oxygens (Figure 2E) and an even wider (11 Å) cavity is formed at the level of IS1.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly provides the measurement of the IS2 site width.

claim: A cavity of 11 Å width is formed at the level of IS1 in the inactivated state.
source: The result is an enlargement of the ion-binding site IS2 to a width of 5.1 Å between opposing carbonyl oxygens (Figure 2E) and an even wider (11 Å) cavity is formed at the level of IS1.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly provides the measurement of the IS1 cavity width.

claim: There are no clear ion densities in the upper selectivity filter of the inactivated state.
source: There are no clear ion densities in the upper selectivity filter.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the absence of ion densities in the upper selectivity filter.

claim: Strong ion densities are seen in IS3 and IS4 in the inactivated Shaker structure.
source: As in the inactivated Shaker structure (Tan et al., 2022) strong ion densities are seen in IS3 and IS4.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly describes the ion densities observed in the inactivated state with citation.

claim: The largest change in the lower binding sites is a rise of 1.3 Å in the position of the G27' carbonyl.
source: The largest change is a rise of 1.3 Å in the position of the G27' carbonyl, the one which defines the top of IS3 (Figure 2J).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly quantifies the conformational change in the lower binding sites.

claim: No evidence of reduced symmetry was detected in the inactivated Kv1.2 channel.
source: However, we were not able to detect any evidence of reduced symmetry in the inactivated Kv1.2 channel.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the absence of symmetry breaking.

claim: The atomic model was built unambiguously into the 2.5 Å map obtained with C4 symmetry imposed.
source: We were able to build the atomic model unambiguously into the 2.5 Å map that was obtained with C4 symmetry imposed.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly describes the model building process.

claim: There was no evidence of broken symmetry when using symmetry expansion and local C1 refinements.
source: Further, there was no evidence of broken symmetry when using symmetry expansion and local C1 refinements of the cryoEM dataset.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly describes the results of symmetry analysis.

claim: Arg300 (R3) is in close proximity to Glu226 on the S2 helix for the open channel.
source: Arg300 (R3) is in close proximity to Glu226 on the S2 helix for the open channel, while R3 is closer to Glu183 in the S2 helix.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly describes the salt bridge interactions in the open state.

claim: The Glu226 side chain adopts a visible interaction with R4 in the inactivated state.
source: The Glu226 side chain adopts a visible interaction with R4 in the inactivated state.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly describes the salt bridge interactions in the inactivated state.

claim: In both open and inactivated states of Kv1.2s, K5 interacts more closely with S2 Phe233 than in the paddle chimera channel.
source: In both open and inactivated states of Kv1.2s, K5 interacts more closely with S2 Phe233 than is the case in the paddle chimera channel (Figure 1E).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly compares the K5-Phe233 interaction between Kv1.2s and the paddle chimera.

claim: There is very little relative movement of residues at the S4-S5 interface between open and inactivated structures.
source: We see very little relative movement of the residues at the S4-S5 interface, much less than 1 Å difference between open and inactivated structures.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly quantifies the structural changes at the S4-S5 interface.

claim: The VSD helix bundle shows an overall rotation of about 3° at the bottom when moving to the inactivated state.
source: When individual VSD domains are aligned the VSD helices in Kv1.2s and the inactivated Kv1.2s-W17'F superimpose very well at the top (including the S4-S5 interface described above), there is a general twist of the VSD helix bundle that yields an overall rotation of about 3° at the bottom of the bundle (Figure 2—figure supplement 3E–F).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly quantifies the VSD rotation.

claim: The axes of helices S0, S1 and S2 tilt by 6°, 4°, and 3.2° in a clockwise direction when moving to the inactivated state.
source: In moving to the inactivated state, the axes of the helices S0, S1 and S2 tilt by 6°, 4°, and 3.2° in a clockwise direction as viewed from the cytoplasmic side, while S4 is stationary.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly quantifies the helix tilting in the inactivated state.

claim: Neither Shaker nor Kv1.2–2.1 structures show VSD rotation between open and inactivated states.
source: In contrast to Kv1.2s, neither Shaker and Kv1.2–2.1 structures show this rotation between open and inactivated states (Figure 2—figure supplement 3G–H) but instead the VSDs remain superimposable.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly compares the VSD behavior across different channel structures.

claim: Alpha-dendrotoxin consists of a peptide chain of 59 amino acids stabilized by three disulfide bridges.
source: Alpha-dendrotoxin (α-DTX) consists of a peptide chain of 59 amino acids stabilized by three disulfide bridges (Figure 3A) and, like other dendrotoxins, exhibits the same fold as Kunitz protease inhibitors (Skarzyński, 1992).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly describes the structure of α-DTX with citation.

claim: Alpha-dendrotoxin exhibits the same fold as Kunitz protease inhibitors.
source: Alpha-dendrotoxin (α-DTX) consists of a peptide chain of 59 amino acids stabilized by three disulfide bridges (Figure 3A) and, like other dendrotoxins, exhibits the same fold as Kunitz protease inhibitors (Skarzyński, 1992).
evidence: The manuscript cites Skarzyński, 1992 for the structural fold of α-DTX.

claim: Modification of Lys5 by acetylation markedly reduces α-DTX binding.
source: The Lys5 side chain protrudes from the surface of the molecule, and its modification by acetylation markedly reduces binding (Harvey et al., 1997).
evidence: The manuscript cites Harvey et al., 1997 for the effect of Lys5 acetylation on binding.

claim: Replacement of Lys5 by alanine decreased the affinity for potassium channels by 1000-fold.
source: Replacement of Lys5 by alanine or ornithine decreased the affinity for potassium channels by 1000-fold and 100-fold, respectively, suggesting that the sidechain geometry is critical (Gasparini et al., 1998).
evidence: The manuscript cites Gasparini et al., 1998 for the mutagenesis data.

claim: Replacement of Lys5 by ornithine decreased the affinity for potassium channels by 100-fold.
source: Replacement of Lys5 by alanine or ornithine decreased the affinity for potassium channels by 1000-fold and 100-fold, respectively, suggesting that the sidechain geometry is critical (Gasparini et al., 1998).
evidence: The manuscript cites Gasparini et al., 1998 for the mutagenesis data.

claim: A C1 reconstruction of α-DTx bound to Kv1.2s was obtained at 3.2 Å resolution.
source: From our cryoEM data we obtained a C1 map of α-DTx bound to Kv1.2s at 3.2 Å; this was done by extensive image processing and was helped by the larger size of α-DTx (59 residues as compared to 35 for ShK).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the resolution of the DTx-bound structure.

claim: The side chain of toxin residue K5 extends with the terminal amine directly coordinated by the Y17' carbonyls.
source: With this map, the side chain of the toxin residue K5 could be traced, apparently with the terminal amine directly coordinated by the Y17' carbonyls.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly describes the structural observation of K5 coordination.

claim: The positively-charged toxin is tethered to the negatively-charged outer mouth of the pore by three salt bridges.
source: The positively-charged toxin is tethered to the negatively-charged outer mouth of the pore by three salt bridges: toxin residues K30, R15, and R3 bind to three channel residues D355, D363, and D363 (D6', D14', and D14' in the turret and pore helix).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly describes the salt bridge interactions between DTx and the channel.

claim: Each of the three channel residues involved in salt bridges with DTx is located on a different subunit.
source: Each of the three channel residues is located on a different subunit (Figure 3G and H).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly describes the subunit arrangement of the salt bridge residues.

claim: In the DTx-bound selectivity filter, a large density peak is seen in a somewhat offset IS1 binding site.
source: In the selectivity filter a large density peak, presumably a K+ ion, is seen in a somewhat offset IS1 binding site; a second, larger K+ ion peak is seen in IS3.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly describes the ion densities observed in the DTx-bound structure.

claim: A second, larger K+ ion peak is seen in IS3 in the DTx-bound selectivity filter.
source: In the selectivity filter a large density peak, presumably a K+ ion, is seen in a somewhat offset IS1 binding site; a second, larger K+ ion peak is seen in IS3.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly describes the ion densities observed in the DTx-bound structure.

claim: No evidence of bound toxin density was found when mixing α-DTX with Kv1.2s W366F protein.
source: We also tried mixing an excess of α-DTX with the Kv1.2s W366F protein sample in an attempt to observe a pore-blocker-bound inactivated structure. However, we found no evidence of bound toxin density on the channel in the cryoEM 2D classes.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the absence of toxin binding to the inactivated channel.

claim: The X-ray crystal structure of KcsA in low K+ solution shows a collapsed selectivity filter.
source: The X-ray crystal structure of the KcsA channel in low K+ solution (Zhou et al., 2001) shows a collapsed selectivity filter, in which the residues V26' and G27' are rearranged, abolishing the binding sites IS2 and IS3.
evidence: The manuscript cites Zhou et al., 2001 for the KcsA structure in low K+.

claim: In low K+, the collapsed KcsA selectivity filter has residues V26' and G27' rearranged, abolishing binding sites IS2 and IS3.
source: The X-ray crystal structure of the KcsA channel in low K+ solution (Zhou et al., 2001) shows a collapsed selectivity filter, in which the residues V26' and G27' are rearranged, abolishing the binding sites IS2 and IS3.
evidence: The manuscript cites Zhou et al., 2001 for the structural details of the collapsed selectivity filter.

claim: Shaker channels conduct Na+ in the absence of K+.
source: On the other hand, Shaker channels are seen to conduct Na+ in the absence of K+ (Melishchuk et al., 1998).
evidence: The manuscript cites Melishchuk et al., 1998 for the Na+ conduction in Shaker.

claim: Large voltage-dependent Na+ currents are observed in wildtype Kv2.1 channels in the absence of K+.
source: In the absence of K+, large voltage-dependent Na+ currents are observed in wildtype Kv2.1 channels (Korn and Ikeda, 1995) and in Shaker channels (Melishchuk et al., 1998).
evidence: The manuscript cites Korn and Ikeda, 1995 for Na+ currents in Kv2.1.

claim: The Kv1.2 structure in Na+ solution shows a selectivity filter conformation little changed from the K+-bound structure.
source: We were surprised to find that it is little changed from the K+-bound structure, with an essentially identical selectivity filter conformation (Figure 4B, Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly describes the structural similarity between K+ and Na+ bound states.

claim: Na+ and K+ ions cannot be distinguished in the density maps.
source: Unfortunately, Na+ and K+ ions cannot be distinguished in the density maps, and we therefore cannot rule out the possibility that peaks in the selectivity filter region might come from contaminating K+ ions.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly acknowledges the limitation in distinguishing Na+ from K+ ions.

claim: The Shaker-W17'F channel in the absence of K+ stably carries large Na+ and Li+ currents.
source: The Shaker-W17'F channel in the absence of K+ stably carries large Na+ and Li+ currents (Starkus et al., 1997).
evidence: The manuscript cites Starkus et al., 1997 for the functional properties of Shaker-W17'F.

claim: The Kv1.2-W17'F channel in Na+ solution has a highly unstable conformation.
source: We conclude that this channel, at least as solubilized in detergent, has a highly unstable conformation when K+ ions are absent.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly concludes about the structural instability based on observations.

claim: The potassium channel signature sequence TTVGYGD was first identified as critical for potassium selectivity.
source: The potassium channel signature sequence TTVGYGD was first identified by Heginbotham et al., 1994 as critical for potassium selectivity.
evidence: The manuscript cites Heginbotham et al., 1994 for the identification of the signature sequence.

claim: The P-loop forms four ion binding sites through which K+ ions and water molecules can pass sequentially in a knock-on fashion.
source: The P-loop (residues 24'–30' in this numbering, TTVGYGD) forms four ion binding sites (Doyle et al., 1998) through which K+ ions and water molecules can pass sequentially in a knock-on fashion.
evidence: The manuscript cites Doyle et al., 1998 for the ion binding sites and conduction mechanism.

claim: C-type inactivation causes channel currents to switch off spontaneously after the opening of the intracellular activation gate.
source: After the opening of the intracellular activation gate formed by the S6 helices, C-type inactivation (Hoshi et al., 1991) causes channel currents to switch off spontaneously.
evidence: The manuscript cites Hoshi et al., 1991 for C-type inactivation.

claim: The inactivation process is very sensitive to mutations in the selectivity filter and nearby residues of the P-region.
source: The inactivation process is very sensitive to mutations in the selectivity filter and nearby residues of the P-region and is influenced by the state of the S6 gate (Cuello et al., 2017; Li et al., 2021a) and the VSDs (Bassetto et al., 2021; Conti et al., 2016).
evidence: The manuscript cites multiple references for the sensitivity of inactivation to mutations.

claim: Low K+ concentrations, especially in the extracellular solution, accelerate inactivation.
source: Low K+ concentrations, especially in the extracellular solution, accelerate inactivation (Levy and Deutsch, 1996).
evidence: The manuscript cites Levy and Deutsch, 1996 for the effect of low K+ on inactivation.

claim: NaK can be converted to a highly K+ selective channel (NaK2K) through the two mutations D28'Y and N30'D.
source: NaK can however be converted to a highly K+ selective channel, termed NaK2K, through just the two mutations D28'Y and N30'D, yielding the P-loop sequence TVGYGD.
evidence: The manuscript describes the mutations that convert NaK to NaK2K, citing Sauer et al., 2011.

claim: NaK2K has the four-site selectivity filter seen in all K+-selective channels.
source: NaK2K has the four-site selectivity filter seen in all K+-selective channels, and the residues Y28' and D30' participate in a hydrogen-bonded network to stabilize the selectivity filter just as in KcsA channels (Doyle et al., 1998).
evidence: The manuscript describes the selectivity filter structure of NaK2K with citations.

claim: The removal of K+ ions from NaK2K destabilizes the selectivity filter, resulting in large fluctuations of the outer pore.
source: Similarly, the removal of K+ ions from NaK2K destabilizes the selectivity filter, resulting in large fluctuations of the outer pore (Matamoros et al., 2023).
evidence: The manuscript cites Matamoros et al., 2023 for the effect of K+ removal on NaK2K.

claim: The standard four-ion-site, K+ selective configuration of potassium channel selectivity filters is an energetically unfavorable, strained backbone conformation.
source: Sauer et al., 2011 conclude that the standard four-ion-site, K+ selective configuration of potassium channel selectivity filters is an energetically unfavorable, strained backbone conformation, and the weakening of the specific interactions that hold it in place lead to its unraveling, producing a lower-energy configuration that yields a nonselective conduction path.
evidence: The manuscript cites Sauer et al., 2011 for this conclusion about selectivity filter energetics.

claim: A large expansion of the outer selectivity filter in W17'F mutants is seen in structures of Shaker, Kv1.2–2.1 channels and Kv1.2.
source: A large expansion of the outer selectivity filter in W17'F mutants is seen in structures of Shaker (Tan et al., 2022), Kv1.2–2.1 channels (Reddi et al., 2022) and also in Kv1.2 as reported here.
evidence: The manuscript describes the structural observation across multiple channel types with citations.

claim: The expansion in Shaker is from 8.6 to 12.8 Å as measured by the distance between diagonally-positioned Y28' alpha-carbons.
source: Quantified as the distance between the diagonally-positioned Y28' alpha-carbons, the expansion in Shaker is from 8.6 to 12.8 Å.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly quantifies the expansion in Shaker.

claim: In both Kv1.2–2.1 paddle chimera and Kv1.2s, the expansion is approximately from 7.2 to 10.7 Å.
source: In both the Kv1.2–2.1 paddle chimera (Reddi et al., 2022) and in Kv1.2s the expansion is approximately from 7.2 to 10.7 Å.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly quantifies the expansion in Kv1.2-2.1 and Kv1.2s.

claim: MD simulations based on the Shaker W434F structure observed simultaneous occupancy of IS3 and IS4 by two K+ ions with high probability.
source: A striking feature of the inactivated state structure reported by Reddi et al., 2022; Tan et al., 2022 is the high occupancy by potassium ions of the two remaining binding sites IS3 and IS4. During normal conduction, ion binding sites in the selectivity filter are usually occupied by K+ and water molecules in alternation (Morais-Cabral et al., 2001). However, in molecular-dynamics simulations based on their Shaker W434F structure, Tan et al., 2022 observed with high probability the simultaneous occupancy of IS3 and IS4 by two K+ ions.
evidence: The manuscript cites Tan et al., 2022 for the MD simulation results.

claim: The ions did not leave the IS3 and IS4 sites during a 2 µs simulation with 300 mV membrane potential applied.
source: The ions did not leave the sites during a (relatively long) 2 µs simulation with 300 mV membrane potential applied, but knock-on permeation events were observed at a low rate, two events during 1µs, at the very high potential of 450 mV.
evidence: The manuscript cites Tan et al., 2022 for the MD simulation results.

claim: Brief 1ms openings of Shaker W17'F channels occurred with a peak open probability of 10^-5 immediately following depolarization to +80 mV.
source: In a study of the Shaker mutant W17'F, Yang et al., 1997 observed, with symmetrical high K+ concentrations to maximize channel activity, brief (1ms) openings of channels that occurred with a peak open probability of 10–5 immediately following a large depolarization to +80 mV (Yang et al., 1997).
evidence: The manuscript cites Yang et al., 1997 for the functional measurements.

claim: When open, the single-channel currents of Shaker W17'F were the same magnitude as the currents in wildtype channels.
source: When open, the single-channel currents were the same magnitude as the currents in wildtype channels.
evidence: The manuscript cites Yang et al., 1997 for the single-channel current measurements.

claim: In the absence of external potassium ions, the peak open probability of Shaker W17'F drops to about 10^-7.
source: In the absence of external potassium ions, the peak open probability drops to about 10–7 (Yang et al., 1997).
evidence: The manuscript cites Yang et al., 1997 for the effect of K+ removal on open probability.

claim: There is little difference in gating-charge movement between Shaker and Shaker W17'F channels.
source: There is however little difference in gating-charge movement between Shaker and Shaker W17'F channels, although Shaker with certain mutations in S4 and S6 do show differences (Bassetto et al., 2021; Conti et al., 2016).
evidence: The manuscript cites references for the gating-charge measurements.

claim: With increased opening of the inner bundle gate in KcsA, there is an increased steric clash between residues of the M2 helix and residues on the pore helix that could lead to inactivation.
source: Such a coupling is clearly seen in a series of KcsA X-ray structures by Cuello et al., 2017: with increased opening of inner bundle gate there is an increased steric clash between residues of the M2 helix and residues on the pore helix that could lead to inactivation.
evidence: The manuscript cites Cuello et al., 2017 for the structural coupling mechanism.

claim: The human Kv1.3 channel was found to spontaneously exist in one or two alternative conformations that appear to be inactivated states.
source: In recent cryoEM studies (Selvakumar et al., 2022) the human Kv1.3 channel was found to spontaneously exist in one or two alternative conformations that appear to be inactivated states.
evidence: The manuscript cites Selvakumar et al., 2022 for the Kv1.3 conformational states.

claim: The D1 conformation of Kv1.3 shows a large displacement of D30' and is reminiscent of the Kv1.3 H20'N mutant structure.
source: The D1 conformation shows a large displacement of D30' and is reminiscent of the cryoEM structure of the Kv1.3 rapidly-inactivating mutant H20'N (Liu et al., 2021).
evidence: The manuscript cites Liu et al., 2021 for comparison with the Kv1.3 mutant structure.

claim: The D2 conformation of Kv1.3 is very similar to the W17'F variant structures.
source: Meanwhile the D2 conformation is very similar to that of the W17'F variants considered here.
evidence: The manuscript compares the D2 conformation to W17'F structures.

claim: The mutation S22'T in the Kv1.2 background has little effect on inactivation.
source: It turns out that the mutation S22'T in the Kv1.2 background has little effect on inactivation; thus to a first approximation the conducting state is equivalently stabilized.
evidence: The manuscript describes the functional effect of the S22'T mutation.

claim: The spider toxins Hanatoxin, SGTx1 and VSTx1 interact with the voltage sensors of Kv channels to inhibit voltage-dependent channel activation.
source: The spider toxins Hanatoxin, SGTx1 and VSTx1 interact with the voltage sensors of Kv channels to inhibit voltage-dependent channel activation (Lee and MacKinnon, 2004; Wang et al., 2004).
evidence: The manuscript cites references for the mechanism of spider toxin action.

claim: The cone-snail toxin Cs1 is thought to block currents by inducing a conformational change in the protein, collapsing the selectivity filter.
source: The cone-snail toxin Cs1 binds to the extracellular surface of Kv channels and is thought to block currents by inducing a conformational change in the protein, collapsing the selectivity filter (Karbat et al., 2019).
evidence: The manuscript cites Karbat et al., 2019 for the mechanism of Cs1 toxin action.

claim: Charybdotoxin blocks Kv1.2-paddle chimera channels by inserting a lysine residue directly into the selectivity filter.
source: In X-ray crystal structures the scorpion toxin Charybdotoxin is seen to block Kv1.2-paddle chimera channels by inserting a lysine residue directly into the selectivity filter, disrupting the ion-binding site IS1 to inhibit ion flow (Banerjee et al., 2013).
evidence: The manuscript cites Banerjee et al., 2013 for the CTx blocking mechanism.

claim: The sea anemone toxin ShK blocks Kv1.3 by the same mechanism as Charybdotoxin.
source: The same mechanism holds for block of Kv1.3 by the sea anemone toxin ShK as studied by cryoEM (Selvakumar et al., 2022); in the latter two cases, the lysine terminal amine interacts with the Y17' carbonyls which form the top of binding site IS1.
evidence: The manuscript cites Selvakumar et al., 2022 for the ShK blocking mechanism.

claim: Block by α-DTx is by occlusion of the selectivity filter through binding of the Lys5 terminal amine.
source: We conclude that block by α-DTx is occlusion of the selectivity filter through binding of the Lys5 terminal amine.
evidence: The manuscript concludes about the blocking mechanism based on structural observations.

claim: Substitution of alanine for Leu9 in α-DTx results in a 1000-fold reduction in toxin affinity.
source: Like the nearby Lys5 residue, substitution of alanine for Leu9 also results in a 1000-fold reduction in toxin affinity (Gasparini et al., 1998).
evidence: The manuscript cites Gasparini et al., 1998 for the mutagenesis data.

claim: The Leu9 sidechain does not show contacts with either the channel or other residues in the toxin itself.
source: In the structure, however, the Leu9 sidechain does not show contacts with either the channel or other residues in the toxin itself.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly describes the structural observation regarding Leu9.

claim: No evidence of bound toxin density was found when mixing α-DTX with Kv1.2s W366F protein.
source: However, we found no evidence of bound toxin density on the channel in the cryoEM 2D classes.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the absence of toxin binding to the inactivated mutant.

claim: Binding of ShK toxin derivative to Kv1.3 occurs to inactivated channels and restores the selectivity filter to its conducting configuration.
source: It should be noted however that in the case of a ShK toxin derivative binding to the Kv1.3 channel, Tyagi et al., 2022 observed that binding occurs to inactivated channels. In that case the inactivated state has a less drastically remodeled selectivity filter, and binding of the toxin restores the selectivity filter to its conducting configuration (Tyagi et al., 2022).
evidence: The manuscript cites Tyagi et al., 2022 for the toxin binding to inactivated Kv1.3.

claim: The conformation of the entire transmembrane region of the Kv1.2 channel appears to be remarkably insensitive to its environment, whether lipid or detergent.
source: Thus, the conformation of the entire transmembrane region of the Kv1.2 channel and its variants appears to be remarkably insensitive to its environment, whether lipid or detergent.
evidence: The manuscript concludes about structural stability based on comparison of structures in different environments.

claim: The Kv1.2s construct contains three mutations in disordered regions of the N-terminus and S1-S2 linker.
source: For this study, we employed a full-length Kv1.2 α-subunit construct containing three mutations in disordered regions of the N-terminus and S1-S2 linker. We denote this construct used for structure determination Kv1.2s.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly describes the construct used for structure determination.

claim: Each β2-subunit contained five mutations chosen to neutralize positive charges on the cytoplasmic face of the subunit.
source: Each β2-subunit contained five mutations chosen to neutralize positive charges on the cytoplasmic face of the subunit; these remove strong, interfering interactions with cryoEM carbon substrates.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly describes the mutations in the β2-subunit and their purpose.

claim: The mutations in the β2-subunit have no effect on β-subunit secondary structure.
source: We find that the mutations have no effect on β-subunit secondary structure.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the structural effect of the β2 mutations.

claim: Many α4 complexes were observed along with the expected α4β4 particles in cryoEM micrographs.
source: Although α and β subunits were co-expressed, in cryoEM micrographs we observed many α4 complexes along with the expected α4β4 particles.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly describes the particle populations observed.

claim: The structures of the transmembrane regions of α4 and α4β4 complexes were indistinguishable.
source: As the structures of the transmembrane regions of these two populations of channels were indistinguishable, we combined the two particle sets.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the structural similarity between the two particle populations.

claim: The presence of β2 subunits has very little effect on the structure of the α-subunit T1 domains.
source: This is reasonable as the presence of β2 subunits has very little effect on the structure of the α-subunit T1 domains to which they bind (Gulbis et al., 2000) and also little effect on channel function (Rettig et al., 1994).
evidence: The manuscript cites references for the minimal effect of β2 subunits on structure and function.
